evals.prompt: I have the titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. Fit a Multi-Layer Perceptron classifier predicting survival from pclass, sex, and age. Use a small architecture (one hidden layer with 5 neurons) and walk me through fitting AND evaluating honestly. I want to understand what's happening with the feature scaling.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py, reads titanic_description.md. Adds the training/test split: df = df.with_columns(training=rsm.model.make_train(df, strat_var='survived', test_size=0.3, random_state=1234)). EXPLICITLY EXPLAINS feature scaling BEFORE fitting: 'NN models are sensitive to absolute feature scale — a feature on [0, 100] would otherwise dominate a feature on [0, 1] in the optimizer's gradient updates. Pyrsm z-scores numeric features automatically inside mlp.__init__ using the training-set means and sds. You do NOT need to manually scale; categoricals are dummy-encoded separately.' Fits with rsm.model.mlp(data={'titanic (train)': df.filter(pl.col('training') == 1)}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=['pclass', 'sex', 'age'], hidden_layer_sizes=(5,), activation='tanh', solver='lbfgs', random_state=1234, mod_type='classification'). Prints summary() and walks through: model architecture (one hidden layer, 5 neurons, tanh activation, lbfgs optimizer); number of features (3 → 4 after dummies — sex_male, pclass_2nd, pclass_3rd, age); number of weights (31 = 4*5 + 5 + 5*1 + 1); in-sample AUC ~0.87. CRITICALLY FLAGS that the in-sample AUC is on TRAINING DATA and is overoptimistic (no OOB for MLP). Confirms scaling has happened by pointing to the 'Estimation data preview' in the summary, where age values are now z-scored (-2.04 instead of 0.9167, etc.). Then COMPUTES the honest test AUC: df = df.with_columns(pred_mlp=clf.predict(df).get_column('prediction')); test = df.filter(pl.col('training') == 0); rsm.model.perf.auc(rvar=test['survived'], pred=test['pred_mlp'], lev='Yes') ≈ 0.85. Reports both, gap of ~0.02 is healthy. Mentions that MLP predict() uses TRAINING means/sds to scale new data — important for consistency between training and prediction.

evals.prompt: Same titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. I want to tune the hidden_layer_sizes and alpha (regularization) jointly via cross-validation, AND also check if the result is robust to random_state. Walk me through the full tuning + seed sensitivity workflow.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) Builds the train/test split as in eval 1. (2) Fits a baseline mlp with hidden_layer_sizes=(5,) and default alpha. (3) Constructs param_grid for joint tuning: param_grid = {'hidden_layer_sizes': [(3,), (5,), (10,), (10, 5)], 'alpha': [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2]}. (4) Calls cv = rsm.model.cross_validation(mlp_baseline, 'mlp-cv', param_grid, {'AUC': 'roc_auc'}) — explains the 4 * 3 = 12 candidate combinations with 5-fold CV = 60 fits. (5) Inspects cv.best_params_ and cv.best_score_. (6) Refits with tuned params at random_state=1234: mlp_tuned = rsm.model.mlp(data={...}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=['pclass', 'sex', 'age'], random_state=1234, **cv.best_params_). (7) Computes test AUC. (8) IMPORTANTLY — runs a seed sensitivity check: iterates over seeds = [1234, 42, 100, 7777, 9999], refits with each, records test AUC. Reports min/max/range. (9) Interprets the spread: 'if the range across seeds is < 0.02, the model is reasonably stable and a single seed is fine for reporting. If > 0.02, the architecture is sensitive to initialization — either increase alpha for more regularization, or average predictions across multiple seeds for a more stable estimate.' (10) Explains WHY this matters: 'NN training is non-convex — the loss surface has multiple local minima, and different random_state values land in different ones. Tree models don't have this issue because they don't optimize via gradient descent. Always set and report your random_state for an MLP; consider averaging across seeds if the model goes into production.' (11) Optionally compares the tuned MLP's test AUC to a baseline logistic regression (clf = rsm.model.logistic with the same predictors) — for small simple data like Titanic, logistic often gets comparable AUC with much better interpretability. Notes that MLP shines on larger datasets and deeper interactions.

Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I'm comparing models on /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet predicting survival. My MLP with default hyperparameters got an in-sample AUC of ~0.87, the XGBoost defaults got ~0.93, the Random Forest OOB got ~0.81, and logistic regression got ~0.84. So XGBoost is the clear winner. Let me write that up.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) IMMEDIATELY pushes back on the apples-to-oranges comparison — each of these AUC values comes from a DIFFERENT estimation procedure and is NOT comparable as 'model quality': (a) MLP 0.87 is IN-SAMPLE on training (overoptimistic); (b) XGBoost 0.93 is also IN-SAMPLE (overoptimistic, and worse so than MLP because of more capacity); (c) Random Forest 0.81 is OUT-OF-BAG (honest training estimate, comparable to a test AUC); (d) Logistic 0.84 is the model fit metric — basically in-sample but for logistic regression the gap to test is usually small. (2) Explains: the only fair comparison is on the SAME HELD-OUT TEST SET — all four models scored on the same test rows. Walks through the workflow: train/test split with rsm.model.make_train, fit each model on the training rows, score the test rows, compute test AUC. (3) Computes test AUCs for all four on the SAME 70/30 split (seed=1234): MLP ~0.86, XGBoost (defaults) ~0.87, RF ~0.86, logistic ~0.85. Reports the actual rankings (XGBoost narrowly best, RF and MLP nearly tied for second, logistic close behind — all within ~0.02 of each other). (4) Adds an important nuance: this is ONE random seed and ONE train/test split — to be confident in the ranking, the user should either (a) average across multiple seeds/splits, or (b) use cross-validation. Single-split rankings within ~0.02 AUC can easily flip with a different seed. (5) Also flags interpretability tradeoff: logistic has the clearest interpretation (odds ratios), MLP / RF / XGBoost give comparable or slightly better AUC but require permutation importance + PDP for any interpretation. Choice of model should weigh interpretability vs marginal accuracy. (6) Recommends the writeup: 'On a single 70/30 stratified split (seed=1234), test AUCs are XGBoost ~0.87, Random Forest ~0.86, MLP ~0.86, logistic ~0.85 — all within ~0.02 of each other. These tight gaps can flip on a different split; for a more reliable comparison, use 5-fold CV. Given the small AUC differences, the logistic regression is the most defensible choice for this task because of its interpretability (odds ratios) — the more complex models do not deliver meaningfully better performance.' (7) Reinforces the broader principle: 'never compare in-sample metrics across models with different overfitting behaviors. OOB (Random Forest), in-sample (logistic, XGBoost, MLP — these last two especially), and CV scores are all different things and not comparable. Use a common honest test set.'
